turns.question: We make about 8,000 tonnes a year of post-industrial multilayer film scrap: 60% LDPE, 20% PET, 10% nylon 6 and 10% EVOH by mass. What is the best way to process it to make money, and how would the answer change if we cared most about circularity? We would build a solvent-based recycling plant just for this scrap.
turns.answer:
To evaluate the optimal pathway for your 8,000 tonnes/year multilayer film scrap (60% LDPE, 20% PET, 10% nylon 6, and 10% EVOH), **9 candidate solvent-wash stages require live BioSTEAM process simulations**, which take about 15 seconds each (approximately 135 seconds in total). Because live simulation has not yet been confirmed, nothing has been simulated yet.

### Stream Analysis and Admissible Washes
- **Solvent-extractable polymers**: Only **LDPE** and **EVOH** have qualifying selective solvent washes. The pending simulations evaluate:
  - **LDPE extraction**: Toluene at 100 °C, *p*-xylene at 100 °C, or diphenyl ether at 115 °C (either as the initial wash at 8,000 t/y or following EVOH removal at 7,200 t/y).
  - **EVOH extraction**: Ethylene glycol at 120 °C or propylene glycol at 120 °C (either as the initial wash at 8,000 t/y or following LDPE removal at 3,200 t/y).
- **Residual polymers**: **PET** (20 wt%) and **nylon 6** (10 wt%) have no admissible selective dissolution washes meeting separation and solubility thresholds; they will remain in the solid residual stream sent to downstream processing.

### Plant Setup and Assumed Defaults
- **Facility configuration**: A dedicated plant sized solely for your 8,000 tonnes/year feed (not shared with outside waste streams).
- **Assumed transport distances**: Published default transport distances to downstream facilities were assumed:
  - Landfill: 9.2 miles
  - Incineration: 151 miles
  - Pyrolysis: 1,034 miles
  - Hydrogen gasification: 2,036 miles
  - Energy gasification: on site (0 miles)
- **Downstream disposition**: The PET/nylon 6 residual (and any unextracted polymer) is evaluated across landfill, incineration, pyrolysis, and three gasification pathways (energy recovery, hydrogen production, and hydrogen with carbon capture).
- **Caveats**: Circularity is assessed as a screening index, and downstream-technology datasets are partly recovered.

Please confirm if you would like to proceed with the 9 live BioSTEAM simulations to determine the maximum-profit and maximum-circularity pathways, and let me know if you would like to override any of the downstream transport distances.

Source: Material identities from DISSOLVE's material identity registry; thermodynamic solubility screening from COSMO-RS predictions; plant techno-economics require unconfirmed live BioSTEAM simulations.

turns.question: Yes, go ahead and run whatever simulations you need.
turns.answer:
To maximize profit, the optimal pathway is a **single solvent wash to recover EVOH using ethylene glycol at 120 °C**, sending the remaining solid residual to **incineration with energy recovery**. If circularity is prioritized instead, the optimal pathway shifts to a **two-stage wash extracting LDPE with toluene at 100 °C, then EVOH with propylene glycol at 120 °C**, sending the unrecovered residual to **landfill**. ### Pathway Comparison | Objective | Wash Sequence | Downstream Fate | Annual Profit ($/yr) | Annual Sales ($/yr) | Capital Cost ($/yr) | Operating Cost ($/yr) | Emissions (t CO2e/yr) | Circularity Index | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Max Profit | EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Incineration with energy recovery | 2,620,000 | 5,870,000 | 2,510,000 | 616,000 | 18,900 | 0.486 | | Max Circularity | 1. LDPE (Toluene, 100 °C)
2. EVOH (Propylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill | 437,000 | 11,400,000 | 9,180,000 | 1,770,000 | 2,870 | 0.710 | *Circularity Index: MICRON 5-category index (0 to 1, higher is more circular) evaluating material substitutability, energy demand, greenhouse gas emissions, waste, and water consumption.* ### Key Trade-offs and Process Breakdown - **Why profit favors single-stage EVOH recovery**: Recovered EVOH commands a high market price ($8,100/t) relative to its low feed share (10%), yielding $5.87M in annual revenue with modest capital outlay ($2.51M/yr annualized capital charge). While recovering LDPE (60% of feed at $1,173/t) adds $5.56M in gross sales, the required high-capacity extraction train adds $6.67M/yr in capital charges and raises operating costs, reducing net annual profit by over 80%. - **Why circularity favors two-stage recovery**: Circularity heavily weights polymer retention and virgin resin substitution. Extracting both LDPE (98.0% recovery) and EVOH (91.2% recovery) recirculates ~68% of the total scrap mass as polymer rather than sending it to combustion, elevating the circularity index from 0.486 to 0.710. Sending the residual to landfill produces substantially lower gate-to-gate emissions (2,870 vs. 18,900 t CO2e/yr) than incineration. - **Unrecovered Polymers**: PET (20 wt%) and nylon 6 (10 wt%) have no admissible selective dissolution washes meeting the thermodynamic screening thresholds (minimum 10 wt% target solubility and maximum 3 wt% co-dissolution) among solvents with cost and life-cycle records. Consequently, they remain in the residual stream in both configurations. - **Assumed Defaults**: Costs reflect a dedicated recycling plant sized for this 8,000 t/yr feed. Default transport distances from the published benchmark were assumed: landfill (9.2 miles), incineration with energy recovery (151 miles), pyrolysis (1,034 miles), energy gasification (0 miles, on site), and hydrogen gasification (2,036 miles). Source: Wash economics and gate-to-gate emissions are live BioSTEAM process simulations of the named configurations; thermodynamic separation thresholds are COSMO-RS predictions; downstream technology data are partly recovered published benchmarks, and circularity is evaluated as a screening index.

turns.question: Show the trade-off between profit and emissions.
turns.answer:
The Pareto frontier between gate-to-gate greenhouse gas emissions and annual profit traces three distinct operational configurations:

### Emissions vs. Profit Trade-off (Pareto Frontier)

| Pathway Configuration | Wash Sequence | Downstream Fate | Annual Profit ($/yr) | Gate-to-Gate Emissions (t CO2e/yr) | Circularity Index |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum Emissions | None (Direct disposal) | Landfill (9.2 miles) | -91,900 | 692 | 0.604 |
| Intermediate (Balanced) | EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill (9.2 miles) | 1,820,000 | 1,370 | 0.632 |
| Maximum Profit | EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Incineration with energy recovery (151 miles) | 2,620,000 | 18,900 | 0.486 |

*Circularity Index: MICRON 5-category index (0 to 1, higher is more circular) evaluating material substitutability, energy demand, greenhouse gas emissions, waste, and water consumption.*

### Key Trade-off Observations

1. **Direct Landfill to EVOH Recovery + Landfill**: Adding a single ethylene glycol wash to recover EVOH elevates annual economics from a net loss of $91,900/yr to an operating profit of $1,820,000/yr. Because landfilling generates minimal direct gate-to-gate emissions for polyolefins, emissions increase by only 673 t CO2e/yr (from 692 to 1,370 t CO2e/yr), while circularity reaches its Pareto maximum (0.632).
2. **Landfill to Incineration with Energy Recovery**: Switching the downstream fate of the 7,380 t/yr solid residual (LDPE, PET, and nylon 6) from landfill to energy-recovery incineration yields an additional $796,000/yr in net profit (reaching $2,620,000/yr). However, combusting the fossil-carbon plastic residual drives a nearly 14-fold increase in gate-to-gate emissions (from 1,370 to 18,900 t CO2e/yr) and drops the circularity index to 0.486 due to the emission penalty.
3. **Absence of LDPE Wash on Frontier**: Two-stage wash sequences recovering LDPE alongside EVOH do not appear on the emissions-profit Pareto frontier. The high capital expenditure and thermal energy required to dissolve and desolventize 60 wt% LDPE lower profit without offering an emissions benefit over single-stage EVOH recovery.

Source: Techno-economic and emissions metrics are live BioSTEAM process simulations of the named configurations; thermodynamic separation thresholds are COSMO-RS predictions; downstream technology data are partly recovered published benchmarks, and circularity is evaluated as a screening index.

turns.question: What if we shared a 20,000 tonne per year recycling plant with other producers instead of building our own?
turns.answer:
Sharing a 20,000-tonne-per-year recycling plant with other producers fundamentally changes the economic optimum: **recovering both LDPE and EVOH becomes the most profitable configuration**, increasing annual profit from $2.62M/yr to **$4.61M/yr** while cutting emissions nearly in half. ### Impact of Facility Sharing on Optimal Pathways | Plant Configuration | Objective | Wash Sequence | Downstream Fate | Annual Profit ($/yr) | Annual Sales ($/yr) | Capital Cost ($/yr) | Emissions (t CO2e/yr) | Circularity Index | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Dedicated (8,000 t/yr) | Max Profit | EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Incineration with energy recovery | 2,620,000 | 5,870,000 | 2,510,000 | 18,900 | 0.486 | | Shared (20,000 t/yr) | Max Profit | 1. LDPE (Diphenyl ether, 115 °C)
2. EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Incineration with energy recovery | 4,610,000 | 11,700,000 | 5,920,000 | 9,590 | 0.595 | | Dedicated (8,000 t/yr) | Max Circularity | 1. LDPE (Toluene, 100 °C)
2. EVOH (Propylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill | 437,000 | 11,400,000 | 9,180,000 | 2,870 | 0.710 | | Shared (20,000 t/yr) | Max Circularity | 1. LDPE (Toluene, 100 °C)
2. EVOH (Propylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill | 4,170,000 | 11,400,000 | 6,090,000 | 2,840 | 0.711 | *Circularity Index: MICRON 5-category index (0 to 1, higher is more circular), evaluated on a consistent scale using upper bounds from the dedicated run.* ### Key Changes from Scale-Sharing - **Economy of Scale Unlocks LDPE Recovery**: In a dedicated 8,000 t/yr plant, the high annualized capital charge of a large LDPE dissolution line ($6.80M/yr) wiped out the margin of recovering LDPE. In a 20,000 t/yr facility where your scrap pays only its proportional throughput share, the capital charge drops to $4.81M/yr for diphenyl ether (and operating cost drops from $1.21M/yr to $898,000/yr). This makes recovering both LDPE (98.0% recovery) and EVOH (91.2% recovery) highly profitable, doubling revenue to $11.7M/yr. - **Lower Incineration Emissions**: Because 68% of the scrap mass is recovered as resin rather than combusted, the residual sent to incineration shrinks from 7,380 t/yr to 2,560 t/yr (comprising PET and nylon 6). Consequently, profit-optimal gate-to-gate emissions drop by ~49% (from 18,900 to 9,590 t CO2e/yr). - **Circularity at High Profit**: Under the shared facility, the maximum-circularity pathway (LDPE via toluene + EVOH via propylene glycol + residual to landfill) yields an annual profit of **$4.17M/yr** (versus only $437,000/yr in a dedicated plant), meaning prioritizing circularity incurs only a minor economic penalty relative to maximum profit ($4.17M vs. $4.61M/yr). - **Residual Disposition**: PET (20 wt%) and nylon 6 (10 wt%) continue to stay in the residual stream in both scenarios, as neither has admissible selective dissolution washes meeting thermodynamic criteria among costable solvents. Source: Wash economics and gate-to-gate emissions are live BioSTEAM process simulations of the named configurations; thermodynamic separation thresholds are COSMO-RS predictions; downstream technology data are partly recovered published benchmarks, and circularity is evaluated as a screening index.

turns.question: Our landfill is 9 miles away and the incinerator 150 miles, but there are pyrolysis and hydrogen gasification plants only 76 miles away, and an energy-recovery gasifier could sit on our site. Does the best pathway change?
turns.answer:
**The solvent wash sequences do not change, but the downstream fate of the unwashed residual shifts from incineration to hydrogen gasification.** Because the hydrogen gasifier is only 76 miles away (compared to 150 miles for the incinerator), routing the solid residual (PET, nylon 6, and any unrecovered polymer) to **gasification for hydrogen with carbon capture** reduces transport trucking costs ($0.07/t-mile), slightly increasing net annual profit. ### Pathway Optimums with Local Downstream Distances | Plant Basis | Objective | Wash Sequence | Downstream Fate | Annual Profit ($/yr) | Gate-to-Gate Emissions (t CO2e/yr) | Circularity Index | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Shared (20,000 t/yr) | Max Profit | 1. LDPE (Diphenyl ether, 115 °C)
2. EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Hydrogen gasification with CCS (76 miles) | 4,620,000 | 9,840 | 0.490 | | Shared (20,000 t/yr) | Max Circularity | 1. LDPE (Toluene, 100 °C)
2. EVOH (Propylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill (9 miles) | 4,170,000 | 2,840 | 0.711 | | Dedicated (8,000 t/yr) | Max Profit | EVOH (Ethylene glycol, 120 °C) | Hydrogen gasification with CCS (76 miles) | 2,660,000 | 19,600 | 0.349 | | Dedicated (8,000 t/yr) | Max Circularity | 1. LDPE (Toluene, 100 °C)
2. EVOH (Propylene glycol, 120 °C) | Landfill (9 miles) | 437,000 | 2,870 | 0.710 | *Circularity Index: MICRON 5-category index (0 to 1, higher is more circular), evaluated on a consistent scale using upper bounds from the baseline run.* ### Impact of Local Facilities 1. **Why Hydrogen Gasification Replaces Incineration**: - Shipping 2,564 t/yr of residual (in the shared plant) 76 miles instead of 150 miles saves $13,460/yr in freight. Both standard hydrogen gasification and gasification with carbon capture tie on operating profit ($4,620,000/yr), but carbon capture cuts gate-to-gate emissions almost in half relative to standard gasification (9,840 vs. 17,200 t CO2e/yr). - In the dedicated plant (recovering only EVOH), 7,376 t/yr of residual travels to gasification, saving $38,720/yr in transport over incineration and lifting profit to $2,660,000/yr. 2. **Why On-Site Energy Gasification and Pyrolysis Were Not Chosen**: - Although on-site energy gasification eliminates transport entirely (0 miles), hydrogen gasification provides more favorable net utility and chemical conversion balances in the process model, outweighing the 76-mile freight cost. - Pyrolysis incurs higher processing operating expenses while yielding uncredited mixed-oil revenue in the gate-to-gate boundary. 3. **Circularity Optimum Remains Unchanged**: - For both shared and dedicated plants, the maximum-circularity pathway continues to route the unwashed residual to the local **landfill (9 miles)**. Landfilling avoids the thermal conversion emissions of gasification or incineration, preserving a high circularity score (0.711 in the shared facility). Source: Wash techno-economics and gate-to-gate emissions are live BioSTEAM process simulations; downstream transport and technology metrics are derived from the published case study with user-specified distances; circularity is evaluated as a screening index.
